implementation_notes: This is an architectural condition, so no language implements it and none can detect it. The measurement is organisational: count services, count services per team, and — the most informative number — services that have never been deployed independently of another. Deployment coupling is the cleanest evidence that a service is a module, and it is measurable from CI history rather than from opinion. The second measurement is where developer effort goes: time spent on service infrastructure, cross-service debugging and pipeline maintenance versus time spent on features. Diagnosis uses tracing data: the clusters of services that call each other in nearly every operation are the consolidation candidates, and the most incident-prone cluster is the one to merge first. The governance answer is a small set of enforceable rules — no production service without an owner, on-call policy and runbook; no new service without a cost attribution and a unit-cost hypothesis; no public API without versioning and deprecation dates — plus explicit lifecycle states so retirement is scheduled rather than never.
idiom_name: service catalogue with mandatory ownership; consolidation as a routine operation
code_sketch:
# the measurement that decides it: deployment coupling
services that were never deployed independently  -> modules, merge them
services with no owner                          -> legacy, assign or retire
cross-cutting change touches N services       -> platform mechanism needed
# the rule that stops the growth
no production service without owner, on-call policy, runbook
no new service without cost attribution tag + unit cost hypothesis
no public API without versioning and deprecation dates
pitfalls: Counting services as the metric; governability is the criterion and the count is only a proxy.
Identifying bounded contexts with service boundaries and producing 50 services in a domain with 8.
Promoting a technical function to a service (logging, validation, caching) instead of making it a library or sidecar.
Continuing to create services while implementing governance, which doubles the backlog.
